newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus plunges in half-year period.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus plunges in half-year period.

text.p: Japan's trade surplus, often a source of contention with the United States, plunged more than 41 percent on a year-on-year basis in the April-September period.

Japan's unadjusted customs-cleared trade surplus in the period, which is the first half of the fiscal year, fell 41.6 percent to 2.90 trillion yen ($25.8 billion), the Finance Ministry announced on Friday.
Healthy growth in imports, which rose 25 percent in the six-month period in value terms, helped to erode the huge surplus.
For example, the surplus with the United States in the six months fell 24.2 percent from a year ago to 1.56 trillion yen ($13.9 billion), thanks to a 29 percent jump in imports.
Meanwhile, Japan had a trade deficit of 1.13 trillion yen ($10 billion) with China as imports from the Asian economic power burgeoned by 35.4 percent from previous-year levels.

Japan's imports from its Asian neighbours are increasing rapidly as Japanese manufacturers, burdened by high costs at home and a strong yen, have been moving their production bases to other countries.

A strong yen makes Japanese products less competitive in overseas markets because it makes them more expensive in foreign currency. The yen hit a record high of 79.75 to the dollar in April 1995 but since then it has slipped against the U.S. currency, trading at around 112 per dollar on Friday.
The ministry also announced Japan's most recent monthly trade data on Friday.

The surplus for September dropped 30.3 percent from the same month a year earlier to 779.52 billion yen ($6.96 billion) -- a number at the lower end of expectations. A Reuters poll of economists had found forecasts ranging between 720 billion yen ($6.42 billion) and 906 billion yen ($8.08 billion).
The latest data showed the trade surplus had declined from year-ago levels for 22 straight months.
Economists agreed that although the surplus was continuing to shrink steadily, the pace of the drop was slowing down.

"I think it (the September figure) is a reminder that the pace of the decline is going to moderate somewhat. Oil prices will keep downward pressure on the trade surplus, but it seems the period of trade adjustment is drawing to a close," said Chris Calderwood, chief economist at BZW Securities Japan.
"It (the surplus) could well stop falling by the beginning of 1997," he told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
In September, imports rose 14.6 percent year on year, a more modest increase than in recent months.
Some economists said there was little need to be alarmed by the slowing drop in the trade surplus.

"I don't think anybody should be unhappy about these figures. They are very good for everyone...the balance with the United States is coming down nicely...all the trade agreements between Japan and the United States are beginning to take effect," Chris Pavlou, Treasurer of global markets at Midland Bank, told RFTV. ($1=112 yen)
